points.title: La concordance des temps dans le discours indirect
points.explanationEn:
Reported speech (discours indirect) means recounting what someone said instead of quoting it directly: instead of 'Il a dit : « Je suis fatigué »' you write 'Il a dit qu'il était fatigué.' The moment you drop the quotation marks and introduce the reported clause with que, French applies a rule called la concordance des temps — tense backshifting — whenever the reporting verb (dire, expliquer, annoncer, répondre, etc.) is itself in a past tense. The tense of the original, directly-quoted sentence shifts back by one 'notch' to reflect that it is now being reported from a later vantage point.

The shifts follow a fixed pattern that is worth memorizing as a table. Présent becomes imparfait: 'Je suis fatigué' → 'qu'il était fatigué.' Passé composé becomes plus-que-parfait: 'J'ai fini' → 'qu'il avait fini.' Futur simple becomes conditionnel présent: 'Je viendrai' → 'qu'il viendrait.' Futur antérieur becomes conditionnel passé: 'J'aurai terminé' → 'qu'il aurait terminé.' Tenses that already express relative anteriority or hypotheticality — imparfait, plus-que-parfait, and conditionnel (both forms) — do not shift any further; they stay exactly as they were in the original utterance, because there's nowhere further back for them to go.

Crucially, this backshift is triggered by the tense of the REPORTING verb, not by some absolute rule that reported speech must always be in the past. If you report speech using a present-tense reporting verb ('il dit que...', 'elle affirme que...'), no backshift happens at all — the quoted tense is preserved exactly: 'Il dit qu'il est fatigué' (He says he is tired), 'Il dit qu'il viendra' (He says he will come). It is only when the reporting verb itself sits in a past tense (a dit, a expliqué, avait annoncé) that the quoted material must shift backward to stay logically consistent with a report being made after the fact.

Reported speech also drags time and place expressions along with it, and this is where English speakers most often forget a step even when they've nailed the verb tenses. 'Aujourd'hui' becomes 'ce jour-là'; 'hier' becomes 'la veille'; 'demain' becomes 'le lendemain'; 'la semaine prochaine' becomes 'la semaine suivante'; 'maintenant' becomes 'à ce moment-là'; 'ici' becomes 'là'. So 'Je pars demain' reported the next day is not 'il a dit qu'il partirait demain' (which would now mean the wrong day) but 'il a dit qu'il partirait le lendemain' — the deictic anchor moves from the moment of speaking to the moment being narrated.

examples.fr: « Je suis malade. » → Elle a dit qu'elle était malade.
examples.en: "I'm sick." → She said she was sick.

examples.fr: « J'ai perdu mes clés. » → Il a expliqué qu'il avait perdu ses clés.
examples.en: "I lost my keys." → He explained that he had lost his keys.

examples.fr: « Je viendrai demain. » → Il a promis qu'il viendrait le lendemain.
examples.en: "I'll come tomorrow." → He promised he would come the next day.

examples.fr: « J'aurai fini avant midi. » → Elle a annoncé qu'elle aurait fini avant midi.
examples.en: "I will have finished before noon." → She announced she would have finished before noon.

examples.fr: « J'étais très occupé hier. » → Il a répété qu'il était très occupé la veille.
examples.en: "I was very busy yesterday." → He repeated that he had been very busy the day before.

examples.fr: « Je viendrais si j'avais le temps. » → Elle a dit qu'elle viendrait si elle avait le temps.
examples.en: "I would come if I had time." → She said she would come if she had time.
examples.note: Conditionnel présent is unchanged after a past reporting verb.
Reporting verb in the present: no backshift at all.

examples.fr: « Je pars ce soir. » → Elle m'a écrit qu'elle partait ce soir-là.
examples.en: "I'm leaving tonight." → She wrote to me that she was leaving that evening.
examples.note: 'Ce soir' shifts to 'ce soir-là' once reported from a later vantage point.

examples.fr: « Nous nous verrons la semaine prochaine. » → Ils ont dit qu'ils se verraient la semaine suivante.
examples.en: "We'll see each other next week." → They said they would see each other the following week.

commonMistakes: Leaving the time expression untouched after backshifting the verb, e.g. saying 'il a dit qu'il partirait demain' instead of 'le lendemain', which misdates the event.
Applying the backshift even when the reporting verb is in the present ('il dit que' wrongly followed by an imparfait or conditionnel, when the original tense should be preserved).
Confusing futur simple → conditionnel présent with the unrelated 'si-clause' conditionnel, and mixing up which conditionnel form (présent vs passé) corresponds to which original future tense.
Trying to backshift an imparfait, plus-que-parfait, or conditionnel any further, when these tenses are already 'terminal' and simply carry over unchanged.
Forgetting to change first/second person pronouns and possessives to match the new reporting perspective (je → il/elle, mes → ses) while focusing only on the verb tense.
whyItTrips: English also backshifts tenses in reported speech ('I am tired' → 'she said she was tired'), which creates a false sense that the rule is identical — but French additionally distinguishes futur/conditionnel and plus-que-parfait pairings that don't map one-to-one onto the two-tense English system.

The parallel shift in time/place words (aujourd'hui → ce jour-là, demain → le lendemain) has no equivalent habit in English reported speech, where speakers often just keep 'tomorrow' or loosely say 'the next day' inconsistently, so it's easy to forget in French.

Because the backshift depends on the tense of the reporting verb rather than being automatic, learners who over-generalize 'reported speech = past tense' end up incorrectly backshifting even after present-tense reporting verbs.

points.title: Questions et ordres au discours indirect
points.explanationEn:
Reporting a question or a command requires more than just backshifting a tense — it requires restructuring the sentence entirely, because direct questions and imperatives use word orders and forms that cannot survive unchanged inside a que-clause. French handles three distinct cases, each with its own connector.

For yes/no questions (ones that could be answered with oui or non), French drops the est-ce que or inversion and introduces the reported question with si: 'Est-ce que tu viens ?' becomes 'Il m'a demandé si je venais.' Watch the elision rule here: si elides to s' before il/ils (s'il vient) but never before elle/elles (si elle vient) — this is one of the few elisions in French that applies to only some of the vowel-initial pronouns, so it has to be memorized rather than assumed to be automatic.

For information questions — the ones built with an interrogative word like où, quand, pourquoi, comment, qui, or combien — that interrogative word is simply carried over into the reported clause, again with the inverted or est-ce que structure stripped away: 'Où vas-tu ?' becomes 'Il m'a demandé où j'allais'; 'Pourquoi es-tu parti ?' becomes 'Il m'a demandé pourquoi j'étais parti.' The two exceptions to watch for are que and qu'est-ce que/qui, which do not carry over as themselves. 'Qu'est-ce que tu fais ?' / 'Que fais-tu ?' (What are you doing?) becomes 'Il m'a demandé ce que je faisais' — the invariant pronoun ce que stands in for 'what' as a direct object. 'Qu'est-ce qui se passe ?' (What's happening?) becomes 'Il m'a demandé ce qui se passait' — ce qui stands in for 'what' as the subject. Mixing these two up (using ce que where the 'what' is the subject of the verb, or vice versa) is a very frequent and noticeable error, so it helps to test which one you need by checking whether 'what' is doing the action (ce qui) or receiving it (ce que).

For commands, French cannot use the imperative inside a reported clause at all — instead it nominalizes the instruction using de + infinitive after a verb like dire, demander, or ordonner: 'Viens ici !' becomes 'Il m'a dit de venir ici.' Negative commands follow the same pattern with ne pas wrapped around the infinitive: 'Ne pars pas !' becomes 'Il m'a dit de ne pas partir.' Note that unlike reported statements and questions, reported commands don't use que at all — the whole construction pivots on de + infinitive, which functions here the way that-clauses with a subjunctive-flavored obligation might in English ('he told me to leave' rather than 'he told me that I should leave').

examples.fr: « Est-ce que tu as fini ? » → Elle m'a demandé si j'avais fini.
examples.en: "Have you finished?" → She asked me if I had finished.

examples.fr: « Viendras-tu à la fête ? » → Il m'a demandé si je viendrais à la fête.
examples.en: "Will you come to the party?" → He asked me if I would come to the party.

examples.fr: « Où habites-tu ? » → Elle m'a demandé où j'habitais.
examples.en: "Where do you live?" → She asked me where I lived.

examples.fr: « Qu'est-ce que tu veux ? » → Il m'a demandé ce que je voulais.
examples.en: "What do you want?" → He asked me what I wanted.

examples.fr: « Qu'est-ce qui te dérange ? » → Elle m'a demandé ce qui me dérangeait.
examples.en: "What's bothering you?" → She asked me what was bothering me.

examples.fr: « Vient-il demain ? » → J'ai demandé s'il venait le lendemain.
examples.en: "Is he coming tomorrow?" → I asked if he was coming the next day.

examples.fr: « Ferme la porte ! » → Le professeur m'a dit de fermer la porte.
examples.en: "Close the door!" → The teacher told me to close the door.

examples.fr: « Ne touchez pas à ça ! » → On nous a dit de ne pas toucher à ça.
examples.en: "Don't touch that!" → We were told not to touch that.

examples.fr: « Pourquoi n'es-tu pas venue ? » → Il m'a demandé pourquoi je n'étais pas venue.
examples.en: "Why didn't you come?" → He asked me why I hadn't come.

examples.fr: « Asseyez-vous. » → L'agent nous a ordonné de nous asseoir.
examples.en: "Sit down." → The officer ordered us to sit down.
examples.note: Reflexive imperative → de + reflexive infinitive, pronoun matches the new subject.

commonMistakes: Trying to keep est-ce que or inversion inside the reported clause instead of collapsing a yes/no question down to 'si'.
Using 'ce que' for a subject question ('what is happening') or 'ce qui' for an object question, instead of correctly matching subject-'what' to ce qui and object-'what' to ce que.
Reporting a command with 'que' plus a conjugated verb instead of switching to 'de' plus the infinitive.
Eliding 'si' before 'elle' (writing 's'elle') by over-applying the s'il elision rule to a pronoun it doesn't apply to.
Forgetting to also apply tense backshift and pronoun changes inside reported questions and commands, treating the restructuring as the only thing that needs to change.
whyItTrips: English reported questions keep a 'wh-word + subject + verb' shape that looks superficially similar to French, which masks the fact that French requires a completely different connector (si) for yes/no questions rather than reusing any question word.

English 'what' does double duty as both subject and object in questions, so English speakers have no built-in reason to distinguish ce qui from ce que — French forces a distinction that English never marks.

English reported commands often keep an infinitive too ('he told me to leave'), which luckily matches French de + infinitif in form, but this false-friend similarity can mislead learners into thinking any French request or order can skip 'de', when it is in fact obligatory.
